title: Medical Terminology
summary: Learn the language of health care: building medical words from roots, prefixes and suffixes, terms for each body system, anatomical directions, diagnostic and procedure terms, safe abbreviations, plurals and plain-language communication.
audience: Health students, medical secretaries, records officers, pharmacy assistants, interpreters and carers

body.p: Most medical terms are built from Greek and Latin word parts. Learning a few hundred parts lets you understand thousands of words, read health records and communicate precisely.

body.h: The parts of a medical word

list: Root: the core meaning, often a body part. cardi = heart, gastr = stomach, hepat = liver, nephr or ren = kidney, oste = bone, derm = skin.
Combining vowel, usually o, links parts for easier pronunciation: cardi/o/logy.

Suffix at the end: -itis (inflammation), -ectomy (surgical removal), -otomy (cutting into), -ostomy (creating an opening), -logy (study of), -algia (pain), -emia (blood condition), -scopy (looking inside with an instrument).
Prefix at the start: hyper- (above, excessive), hypo- (below, deficient), tachy- (fast), brady- (slow), dys- (difficult, abnormal), peri- (around), inter- (between), intra- (within).

body.p: Start with the suffix, then read from the beginning. Gastritis: inflammation (-itis) of the stomach (gastr). Cardiology: the study of the heart. Hepatomegaly: enlargement (-megaly) of the liver. Tachycardia: a fast heart rate. Appendectomy: surgical removal of the appendix; colostomy: an opening into the colon.

body.tip: Make flashcards of roots, prefixes and suffixes, then practise building and breaking down real terms from health leaflets.

body.p: Terms cluster around body systems. Knowing the main roots for each system helps you place a word quickly.

list: Cardiovascular: cardi/o (heart), angi/o and vas/o (vessel), arteri/o (artery), ven/o and phleb/o (vein), hem/o and hemat/o (blood).
Respiratory: pneum/o and pulmon/o (lung), bronch/o (bronchus), rhin/o (nose), -pnea (breathing): dyspnea is difficult breathing.
Digestive: or/o (mouth), esophag/o, gastr/o, enter/o (intestine), col/o (colon), hepat/o (liver).
Urinary: nephr/o and ren/o (kidney), cyst/o (bladder), ur/o (urine).
Nervous: neur/o (nerve), encephal/o (brain), my/o (muscle), -plegia (paralysis).
Musculoskeletal: oste/o (bone), arthr/o (joint), chondr/o (cartilage).
Endocrine: thyr/o (thyroid), aden/o (gland), glyc/o (sugar): hyperglycemia means high blood sugar.
Reproductive: gynec/o (woman), hyster/o (uterus), obstetr/o (pregnancy and birth).

body.p: Example: nephrolithiasis breaks down as nephr/o (kidney) + lith (stone) + -iasis (condition): kidney stones.

body.tip: Learn terms system by system alongside basic anatomy; meaning sticks better when you can picture the organ.

body.p: Health workers describe locations on the body precisely, always as if the patient is in the anatomical position: standing upright, facing forward, arms at the sides with palms facing forward.

list: Anterior (ventral): front; posterior (dorsal): back.
Superior: towards the head; inferior: towards the feet.
Medial: towards the midline; lateral: away from the midline.
Proximal: closer to where a limb attaches; distal: further away. The wrist is distal to the elbow.
Superficial: near the surface; deep: further inside.
Sagittal plane: divides left and right; transverse: upper and lower; coronal (frontal): front and back.
Supine: lying on the back; prone: lying face down; lateral: lying on the side.
The abdomen is divided into four quadrants (right upper, left upper, right lower, left lower) or nine regions, to describe pain and findings.

body.p: "Left" and "right" always mean the patient's left and right, not the observer's.

body.tip: When describing a wound or pain, combine terms: "a 2 cm laceration on the lateral aspect of the left distal forearm".

body.p: Many terms describe how conditions are found and treated.

list: -gram: the record or image (electrocardiogram, mammogram); -graphy: the process of recording (radiography); -scopy: viewing with a scope (endoscopy, colonoscopy).
Biopsy: removing tissue for examination under a microscope.
Benign: not cancerous; malignant: cancerous, able to spread; metastasis: spread to another part of the body.
Acute: sudden onset, usually short; chronic: long-lasting.
Signs are objective findings (fever, rash); symptoms are what the patient reports (pain, nausea).
Diagnosis: identifying the condition; prognosis: the likely outcome.
-plasty: surgical repair (rhinoplasty); -pexy: surgical fixation; -tripsy: crushing (lithotripsy breaks stones).

body.p: "An acute appendicitis confirmed by ultrasound was treated with laparoscopic appendectomy" means: a sudden inflammation of the appendix, confirmed by an ultrasound scan, was treated by removing the appendix through small incisions using a camera (lapar/o = abdomen, -scopic = viewing).

body.tip: Collect unfamiliar terms you meet and break each one into parts; most become clear quickly.

body.p: Abbreviations save time but cause errors when misread. Health services keep approved abbreviation lists and lists of abbreviations that must never be used.

list: BP (blood pressure), HR (heart rate), RR (respiratory rate), T (temperature), SpO₂ (oxygen saturation).
Hx (history), Dx (diagnosis), Rx (prescription or treatment), Tx (treatment), Sx (symptoms).
PO (by mouth), IV (intravenous), IM (intramuscular), SC (subcutaneous).
Medication timing abbreviations such as bd (twice daily) and tds (three times daily) are used in some countries, but many services prefer writing timing in full.
"U" for units can be misread as 0 or 4: write "units".
"µg" can be misread as "mg": write "micrograms".
Trailing zeros (5.0 mg) can be read as 50 mg; always use a leading zero for decimals (0.5 mg).
"QD" or "OD" have been confused between "once daily" and "right eye".

body.tip: When in doubt, write it out in full. Clarity is always safer than speed.

lessons.title: Plurals, pronunciation and talking with patients

body.p: Medical words often keep Greek or Latin plurals: diagnosis becomes diagnoses, vertebra becomes vertebrae, bacterium becomes bacteria, ovum becomes ova, nucleus becomes nuclei, and appendix becomes appendices.

list: Some words sound alike but mean different things: ileum (part of the small intestine) and ilium (hip bone); perineal and peroneal.
Misspelling can change meaning, so check spelling carefully in records.
Listen to audio pronunciations from reliable medical dictionaries.

body.p: Medical terms help professionals communicate precisely, but patients need plain language. Say "high blood pressure" rather than "hypertension", or explain the term when you use it. Check understanding by asking the patient to explain back in their own words, and use trained interpreters for patients who speak other languages.
Medical terminology skills are useful for nurses, medical secretaries, health-records officers, pharmacy assistants, medical coders and interpreters.

body.tip: Translate one technical sentence a day into plain words; it improves both your terminology and your patient communication.
